say: You give it fractions or mixed numbers. It gives back one **simplified** fraction.
The key idea: you can only add or subtract fractions with the same denominator, so first rewrite each one over a common denominator.

how.ordinary: Ordinary level never asks for it alone. It is a step inside Paper 1 parts, such as working out a value to give a fraction in a 5 mark part, or adding journey times in a longer question.

example.question: Work out $\frac{5}{6} + \frac{3}{4} - \frac{1}{3}$. Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.

steps.title: Find a common denominator
steps.say: The denominators are $6$, $4$ and $3$. Find the smallest number they all divide into. That is $\hl{1}{12}$. Rewrite each fraction over $\hl{1}{12}$.

lines.text: Multiply top and bottom by the same number each time: by $2$, by $3$ and by $4$.

steps.title: Combine the numerators
steps.say: Now the denominators match. Add and subtract the tops. The bottom stays $\hl{1}{12}$.

steps.title: Simplify
steps.say: Both $15$ and $12$ divide by $3$. Divide top and bottom by $3$.

ordinary.tip: Show the substitution before you work with fractions. Some correct substitution earns partial credit.
If you cannot finish, still start combining. Work towards a single fraction earns marks.
Give the answer in the form the question asks for. A correct value in the wrong form loses a mark.

say: You give it a decimal, terminating or recurring. It gives back the same number as a **fraction**, or the other way round.
The key idea for a recurring decimal: multiply to shift the repeating block, then subtract so the repeating part cancels.

example.question: Write $0.454545\ldots$ as a fraction in its simplest form.

steps.title: Name the number
steps.say: Let $\hl{1}{x}$ be the number. The block $45$ repeats, so it has length two.

steps.title: Shift one block
steps.say: Multiply by $100$ to move the decimal point past one whole block. The repeating part stays the same.

steps.title: Subtract
steps.say: Subtract the first line from the second. The repeating parts cancel exactly.

steps.title: Divide and simplify
steps.say: Divide both sides by $99$. Then divide top and bottom by $9$.

say: You give it a number. It tells you the **smallest** set it belongs to: $\mathbb{N}$, $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Q}$ or $\mathbb{R}$.
The key idea: the sets grow outwards. Each one sits inside the next, so ask the questions in order, from the smallest set up.

how.ordinary: Ordinary level tests it on Paper 1, in 2023 as the main skill of a 5 mark part: graph inequalities on a number line for $\mathbb{N}$, $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{R}$.

example.question:
For each number, write down the smallest of the sets $\mathbb{N}$, $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Q}$, $\mathbb{R}$ that contains it.
$\sqrt{25}$, $-4$, $\frac{3}{8}$, $\sqrt{10}$

steps.title: Simplify the roots
steps.say: Work out any square root that is a whole number. $\sqrt{25}$ is $5$, a counting number.

steps.title: Check for a minus sign
steps.say: $-4$ is a whole number, but it is negative, so it is not in $\mathbb{N}$. Whole numbers with negatives are the integers.

steps.title: Try writing as a fraction
steps.say: $\frac{3}{8}$ is a fraction of two integers, and it is not a whole number. It is in the rationals. Its decimal ends.

steps.title: Look at the decimal
steps.say: $\sqrt{10}$ is not a whole number. Its decimal never ends and never repeats, so it is not a fraction. That makes it irrational.

ordinary.tip: Show that you know what $\mathbb{N}$, $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{R}$ contain. That alone earns partial credit.

ordinary.tip: Graph each inequality for its own set. Getting two of the three correct earns high partial credit.

ordinary.tip: Write $\leq$ where the question has it. Using $\geq$ by mistake costs a star the first time.

say: You give it a natural number. It writes it as a product of **primes**, and uses that to find the HCF and LCM.
The key idea: every number has exactly one prime factorisation. The HCF takes the primes both numbers share. The LCM takes every prime that appears in either.

how.higher: Higher level tested it in 2023 on Paper 1 as a 15 mark part: list the factors of a power of 2, then count the factors of a number like $2^{10} \times 3^{12}$.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level tested it in 2025 on Paper 1 as a 10 mark part: find when two repeating times, every $9$ and every $12$ minutes, line up.

example.question:
(i) Write $252$ and $180$ as products of prime numbers.
(ii) Hence find the HCF and the LCM of $252$ and $180$.

steps.title: Factorise 252
steps.say: Divide by the smallest prime that goes in. Keep going until only primes are left.

steps.title: Find the HCF
steps.say: The HCF uses only the primes in **both** numbers, each to its smaller power. Both have $\hl{1}{2^2}$ and $\hl{1}{3^2}$.

steps.title: Find the LCM
steps.say: The LCM uses every prime in **either** number, each to its larger power. Add the $5$ and the $7$ to the HCF primes.

higher.tip: To count the factors of a number in index form, add $1$ to each power and multiply the results.
Correct answers without work earn full credit, but show the working.
